subtype_label: Focus internal / focus inference (no given focus)
query: Help me understand what's worth attention in these incident descriptions.

judge.implied_focus: Incident triage prioritization -- inferring which incidents (and why) warrant attention based on their nature, severity, and blast radius

per_column.name: problem_domain
per_column.rationale: Classifies the incident into a technical domain (database, email, vpn), a core facet of characterizing what an incident is about and where attention should go.

per_column.name: severity_signal
per_column.rationale: Encodes impact type (outage, access_degraded, infrastructure_failure) -- directly a prioritization/attention signal derived from the description.

per_column.name: scope_context
per_column.rationale: Captures blast radius (enterprise_system, building_wide, single_user), a key attention facet: broad-scope incidents warrant more attention.

per_column.name: caller_recurrence
per_column.rationale: Derived from caller_id metadata rather than the description's substance; only loosely tied to 'what's worth attention' and drifts toward a caller-analytics facet.

per_column.name: technician_workload
per_column.rationale: Describes assignee load, an operational/staffing facet orthogonal to what makes an incident description worth attention; introduces scatter.

judge.rationale: The first three columns cohere tightly around a single inferable focus -- triaging incidents by what/how-bad/how-wide -- forming a genuine multi-facet analytical structure at useful granularity (domain x severity x scope), not a restatement or noise. This focus is clearly actionable: an analyst can prioritize enterprise-wide outages in the database/vpn domains. However, the last two columns (caller_recurrence, technician_workload) pivot away from the description content toward caller/staffing analytics, diluting the single-focus centring and pulling the set partway toward a grab-bag. Hence solid but not maximal coherence and structure.
